These are NOT logically equivalent for general simple graphs. Counterexample: let G have V={1,2,3} and E={{1,2}}, H have the same V and E={{1,2},{2,3}}, and f be the identity bijection. Every G edge maps to an H edge, yet inverse reflection fails for {2,3}, so G and H are NOT isomorphic. obs.wave2.quot118.ordinary-generating-fu.editorial_note: ProofWiki specifically defines generating function of a real sequence as sum of coefficient times nonnegative integer powers, and defines the resulting function only on z where the power series CONVERGES. The current approved context restricts the variable to real z, a mathematical specialization of the source's undifferentiated z; 0 always lies in D for an ordinary n≥0 power series. Do not silently equate this convergent analytic function with a formal power series in R[[z]], which exists independently of convergence and may have a different target object. Nor is this an exponential generating function involving 1/n!, a moment-generating function, or the double-index generating function the page separately describes. The coefficient extraction notation [z^n]G=a_n is a consequence of the power series presentation, not an extra inequivalent definition; uniqueness of analytic coefficients requires the appropriate analytic interpretation. obs.wave2.cross132.convex-hull.02.context: Convex hull of subset U of a real vector space V, three equivalent set constructions / intersection-convex-supersets
obs.wave2.cross132.convex-hull.02.editorial_note: ProofWiki directly lists THREE equivalent descriptions: all finite strictly positive-weight convex combinations of elements of U, intersection of all convex sets containing U, and smallest convex superset. The source additionally has a separate equivalence-of-definitions theorem which was read. These all describe ONE convex hull meaning in a REAL vector space V, for ANY subset U (including empty U), not a closed convex hull, affine hull, or linear span. Positive weights are harmless compared with nonnegative finite convex combinations because terms with zero weight may be discarded; m≥1 means no nonempty convex combination exists for empty U, so conv(∅)=∅. Empty subset is conventionally convex, so intersection of convex supersets for U=∅ also equals ∅, consistent with the finite-combination definition. The convex subset predicate itself is separately needed to fully link formulations 2 and 3; no source-screened target should be invented before discovery. Convex hull need not be closed in infinite-dimensional normed spaces, so closed convex hull is DIFFERENT. Convex combinations are finite, not general countably infinite sums. The least-convex-superset condition is inclusion-minimal plus contained in every convex superset, not any arbitrary minimal convex superset. Source sections: Definition 1 all finite strictly positive coefficient convex combinations, Definition 2 intersection of convex supersets, Definition 3 smallest convex superset, Equivalence of Definitions of Convex Hull checked

obs.wave2.conv125.locally-uniform-conver.editorial_note: ProofWiki explicitly states the general definition: for each point x of topological X there is some neighborhood U_x on which the entire sequence of maps to a metric M converges uniformly. The neighborhood may depend on x, and the uniform N_ε may depend on the chosen U_x as well as ε, but is NOT allowed to vary with individual points y∈U_x. Global uniform convergence implies locally uniform; converse fails on noncompact spaces generally (e.g. f_n(x)=x/n on R converges uniformly on each bounded neighborhood, not uniformly on all R). Local uniformity is stronger than mere pointwise convergence. Source also gives complex-open-disc specialization and locally uniform series via partial sums; those are contexts with additional complex-function or series prerequisites not promoted here. No local compactness, Hausdorff property, or completeness assumed by the general version, except that metric targets are Hausdorff. Empty X satisfies the condition vacuously. Sections: General Definition, Complex Functions open-disk specialization not promoted, Series partial-sum specialization not promoted

obs.wave2.cross132.convex-hull.01.editorial_note: ProofWiki directly lists THREE equivalent descriptions: all finite strictly positive-weight convex combinations of elements of U, intersection of all convex sets containing U, and smallest convex superset. The source additionally has a separate equivalence-of-definitions theorem which was read. These all describe ONE convex hull meaning in a REAL vector space V, for ANY subset U (including empty U), not a closed convex hull, affine hull, or linear span. Positive weights are harmless compared with nonnegative finite convex combinations because terms with zero weight may be discarded; m≥1 means no nonempty convex combination exists for empty U, so conv(∅)=∅. Empty subset is conventionally convex, so intersection of convex supersets for U=∅ also equals ∅, consistent with the finite-combination definition. The convex subset predicate itself is separately needed to fully link formulations 2 and 3; no source-screened target should be invented before discovery. Convex hull need not be closed in infinite-dimensional normed spaces, so closed convex hull is DIFFERENT. Convex combinations are finite, not general countably infinite sums. The least-convex-superset condition is inclusion-minimal plus contained in every convex superset, not any arbitrary minimal convex superset. Source sections: Definition 1 all finite strictly positive coefficient convex combinations, Definition 2 intersection of convex supersets, Definition 3 smallest convex superset, Equivalence of Definitions of Convex Hull checked

obs.wave2.directional112.directional-der.editorial_note: The source juxtaposes a gradient dot unit-direction formula when the gradient 'exists' and a derivative of f(a+tu) under a differentiability assumption, and an equivalence page repeats both. The gradient can be understood as the vector of partial derivatives, which may exist at a point even though f is not differentiable there. Counterexample: f(x,y)=xy/(x²+y²) for (x,y)≠(0,0) and f(0,0)=0 has both coordinate partial derivatives zero at the origin, so ∇f(0,0)=(0,0), but along u=(1,1)/√2, f(tu)=1/2 and the directional difference quotient (1/2)/t fails to have a finite two-sided limit. Thus gradient existence is insufficient and the claimed equivalence requires strengthening, e.g. Fréchet/total differentiability. Source-only record of the suspect gradient alternative is HELD and must not enter approved mathematical meanings. The separately recorded line-restriction definition is mathematically correct under total differentiability, as explicitly required by source Definition 2. Do not conflate with one-sided directional derivatives or gradients in Banach spaces. Sections: Definition 1 gradient formula, Definition 2 differentiable curve restriction, Equivalence of Definitions of Directional Derivative separately inspected

obs.wave2.branch128.product-topology.01.context: Product topology on arbitrary indexed Cartesian product, two equivalent subbasis and finite-support basis descriptions / projection-cylinder-subbasis
obs.wave2.branch128.product-topology.01.editorial_note: The directly read ProofWiki Product Topology page defines the smallest topology making coordinate projections continuous by the SUBBASIS of cylinder preimages π_i^{-1}(U). Its Also See directly states the finite-coordinate-support natural basis; the linked Natural Basis of Product Topology theorem was independently read, and shows equivalence by finite intersections of cylinder sets. Both are equivalent formulations of ONE indexed-product topology, not different meanings. IMPORTANT: the set of individual cylinder preimages is a subbasis, generally NOT the complete topology or a basis closed under finite intersections. The product topology of infinitely many factors is not generally the BOX topology whose product basic open sets may restrict infinitely many coordinates. An empty index set produces a singleton product with unique topology. Empty factor spaces produce an empty product; this definition does not require nonempty factors. Product topology T^D on function space is the special case X_i=T for each index i∈D; this supplies the previously missing pointwise-convergence prerequisite. No Hausdorff, compactness, metric or continuity of maps into X is silently imposed. Sections: General definition by generated inverse-image subbasis, Natural basis using finite coordinate restrictions linked to separate directly inspected theorem https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Natural_Basis_of_Product_Topology, Finite product is specialization

obs.wave2.conv125.pointwise-convergence..editorial_note: ProofWiki explicitly distinguishes real-valued pointwise convergence with ∀x then ∀ε then ∃N from the equivalent topological-space function-product formulation for arbitrary topological T. The real scope requires finite real pointwise limits but does not require uniform N; the quantifier order allows N to depend on x. Its topological product criterion is valid for arbitrary topological spaces using the product topology, including non-Hausdorff targets where limits may not be unique. The two source contexts should NOT be listed as globally equivalent mathematical definitions without explicitly identifying the real metric topology as a specialization; topological version is more general. For empty D, pointwise convergence holds vacuously for every f and every sequence, including the unique empty map. The source allows N∈R rather than N∈N, which is equivalent for integer n; our paraphrase chooses a natural cutoff. Uniform convergence is stronger for real target and is not to be substituted. The product-topology meaning is a separate prerequisite candidate, not fabricated if unscreened. Sections: Definition real-valued ε-N quantifier order, Topological-space section product topology equivalence, Comment comparison with uniform convergence

obs.wave2.directional112.closed-ball.02.editorial_note: ProofWiki defines closed metric and closed norm balls with non-strict distance/norm inequality and a strictly positive real radius. Its overline-ball notation is potentially misleading: in a general metric space, the metric closed ball need not equal the topological closure of the corresponding open ball. For example, a discrete metric space with distances 0 or 1 has open ball B(a,1)={a} and closed ball C(a,1)=X if there is more than one point, hence closure(B(a,1))≠C(a,1). No automatic equivalence between closed metric ball and closure of open metric ball is admitted. The two source contexts agree when the norm generates a metric, but this source does not require completeness or Hilbert structure. A closed ball is topologically closed in any metric space; that is a theorem, not a second defining condition. Sections: Metric Space, Normed Vector Space

obs.wave2.branch128.exponential-generati.editorial_note: The directly inspected ProofWiki Exponential Generating Function page defines G_A(z)=Σ_{n≥0} a_n z^n/n! for a REAL sequence and explicitly restricts the function domain to arguments where the series converges. This approved meaning specializes its z variable to real values and does not claim complex analyticity without sources. It is NOT the ordinary generating function Σa_n z^n of the SAME sequence unless specific coefficient conditions happen to make them coincide. It can be described as an ordinary generating function of a transformed sequence b_n=a_n/n!, but that transformation is a mathematical relation and not a claim that the two generators are synonymous under original coefficients. A formal EGF may be defined without convergence in a separate algebraic context; it is NOT this real-function meaning. For undirected simple graphs, a circuit contains a cycle, making their absence equivalent, even without finiteness; they should share one mathematical meaning with two individually sourced formulations. The source separately mentions rooted tree as an alternative terminology, but the root, parent and child structures are not independently defined here; do not silently turn the unrooted meaning into a rooted tree. A tree can be finite or infinite; do not impose finite vertex set. The empty-graph connectedness convention is not settled by this source and must not be asserted. obs.wave2.real49.02.editorial_note: The representation q↦{r∈Q:r<q} is injective and order-preserving. Under strict lower-cut convention equality of real numbers is literal equality of cuts; abstract real field systems are isomorphic, not literally this set. Do not assert field/completeness without the separate proofs of operations.
obs.wave2.real49.02.text: Let R_D be the set of all lower Dedekind cuts A⊂Q. For cuts A,B define A≤B exactly when A⊆B. The rational number q is represented by the cut {r∈Q:r<q}. With suitably defined addition and multiplication on cuts, R_D forms a complete ordered field.

source.context: Concrete Dedekind-cut realization: real numbers represented by rational lower cuts
source.text: In the Dedekind-cut construction, the underlying set R_D consists of all lower Dedekind cuts A of Q. Define the order by A≤B if and only if A⊆B. Each rational q has the canonical representation {r∈Q:r<q}. Defining arithmetic on cuts and proving the ordered-field axioms and the least-upper-bound property then gives a concrete realization of a real-number system.
